title: What is Programming?
summary: Giving a machine an unambiguous sequence of instructions it can execute.

title: Source Code
summary: Human-written text that a compiler or interpreter turns into behavior.

title: Compiler
summary: A program that translates source into a lower-level form, usually ahead of time.

title: Interpreter
summary: A program that executes source (or bytecode) directly, without a separate machine-code binary.

title: Linker
summary: The tool that combines object files and libraries into a single executable image.

title: Loader
summary: The OS component that maps an executable into memory and starts it.

title: Runtime
summary: The support system a program needs while it runs: memory, threads, I/O, and language services.

title: Variables
summary: Named storage for values. A variable binds a name to a location and a type.

title: Data Types
summary: The set of values a variable can hold and the operations that are legal on them.

title: Operators
summary: Built-in operations: arithmetic, comparison, logic, bitwise, and assignment.

title: Conditions
summary: Control flow that chooses a path from a boolean expression.

title: Loops
summary: Control flow that repeats a block while a condition holds, or over a collection.

title: Functions
summary: Named, reusable units of computation with parameters, a body, and a return.

title: Recursion
summary: A function that solves a problem by calling itself on a smaller instance, with a base case.

title: Scope
summary: The region of a program where a name is visible. Nested scopes shadow outer ones.

title: Call Stack
summary: The region that stores frames for active function calls: locals, return address, saved registers.

title: Heap
summary: The region for dynamically allocated objects whose lifetime is not tied to a single frame.

title: Memory
summary: The addressable store a program reads and writes: code, data, stack, and heap.

title: Pointers
summary: Values that hold addresses. They make aliasing, data structures, and manual memory possible.

title: References
summary: Names that alias an existing object without exposing arithmetic on its address.

title: Dynamic Memory
summary: Allocation whose size or lifetime is decided at run time, not at compile time.

title: Garbage Collection
summary: Automatic reclamation of heap objects the program can no longer reach.

title: Error Handling
summary: How a program detects, reports, and recovers from failures without corrupting state.

title: Exceptions
summary: A non-local control-flow mechanism that unwinds the stack until a handler matches.

title: Debugging
summary: The discipline of forming a hypothesis about a defect and testing it against the running program.

title: File I/O
summary: Reading and writing byte streams that outlive the process: files, pipes, sockets.

title: Modules
summary: Compilation or namespace units that hide internals and export a small interface.

title: Packages
summary: Versioned bundles of modules, with metadata for installation and dependency resolution.

title: Libraries
summary: Reusable code meant to be linked or imported, not run as a program on its own.

title: APIs
summary: The contract a component publishes: types, functions, errors, and the rules for using them.

title: C
summary: A small systems language with manual memory, undefined behavior, and a stable ABI.

title: C++
summary: C’s model plus abstractions: RAII, templates, and zero-cost as a design goal.

title: Java
summary: A managed, class-based language with a VM, a huge standard library, and structured concurrency evolving in.

title: Python
summary: A dynamic language whose object model, iterators, and C-API shape almost every data stack.

title: JavaScript
summary: The language of the web: prototypes, the event loop, and a single-threaded concurrency story.

title: TypeScript
summary: A gradual type system erased at compile time, sitting on top of JavaScript.

title: Go
summary: A small language with goroutines, channels, and a runtime aimed at networked services.

title: Rust
summary: Ownership, borrowing, and a type system that makes aliasing and mutation exclusive.

title: Kotlin
summary: A JVM (and beyond) language with null-safety, coroutines, and Java interop as a first-class goal.

title: Swift
summary: Apple’s language: value types, optionals, ARC, and protocol-oriented design.

title: SQL (Language)
summary: A declarative language for describing the result you want from a relational store.

title: Bash
summary: The default Unix shell language: pipelines, redirection, and the glue of every server.

title: Arrays
summary: A contiguous sequence of elements addressable in O(1) by index.

title: Strings
summary: Sequences of characters. Encoding, immutability, and matching dominate their cost.

title: Linked Lists
summary: Nodes linked by pointers. O(1) insert at a known node, O(n) access by index.

title: Doubly Linked Lists
summary: Each node points both ways, so deletion and reverse traversal do not need a predecessor walk.

title: Circular Linked Lists
summary: The last node points at the first. Useful for round-robin structures and buffers.

title: Stack
summary: Last-in, first-out. Recursion, undo, and parsing are stacks in disguise.

title: Queue
summary: First-in, first-out. BFS, printers, and thread pools are queues.

title: Deque
summary: A double-ended queue: push and pop at both ends in O(1).

title: Hash Tables
summary: Average O(1) insert/lookup via a hash function and a collision strategy.

title: Hash Maps
summary: A hash table used as an associative array from keys to values.

title: Sets
summary: Collections that answer membership. Hash sets and tree sets make different promises.

title: Trees
summary: Connected acyclic graphs with a root. Hierarchical data lives here.

title: Binary Trees
summary: Each node has at most two children. Traversals and shape govern everything else.

title: Binary Search Trees
summary: Left < node < right. Ordered operations in O(h), which is O(log n) if balanced.

title: AVL Trees
summary: BSTs that rebalance on insert/delete so height stays within 1 of a sibling.

title: Red-Black Trees
summary: A weaker balance invariant than AVL, with cheaper updates — the usual map/set backbone.

title: Heaps
summary: Almost-complete binary trees that keep the min or max at the root in O(1).

title: Priority Queues
summary: Extract-min (or max) in O(log n). Dijkstra, schedulers, and A* depend on them.

title: Tries
summary: Trees indexed by characters (or bits). Prefix queries and dictionaries live here.

title: Segment Trees
summary: A tree over ranges that answers range queries and updates in O(log n).

title: Fenwick Trees
summary: A compact prefix-sum tree: range sums and point updates in O(log n).

title: Graphs
summary: Vertices and edges. The universal model for networks, dependencies, and state spaces.

title: Disjoint Set Union
summary: Near-O(1) union and find — the backbone of Kruskal and connected components.

title: Big-O, Theta, Omega
summary: How runtime and memory grow: upper, tight, and lower bounds as n → ∞.

title: Searching
summary: Finding a value in a collection: linear, binary, and hash-based membership.

title: Sorting
summary: Putting elements in order. Stability, adaptivity, and n log n lower bounds matter.

title: Binary Search
summary: Halve a monotonic search space until the answer remains. The idea is bigger than arrays.

title: Two Pointers
summary: Two indices walking a sequence to find pairs, partitions, or a window in linear time.

title: Sliding Window
summary: A subarray that grows and shrinks to maintain a constraint while scanning once.

title: Prefix Sum
summary: Precomputed partial sums so any range sum is two lookups.

title: Recursion (Algorithms)
summary: The algorithmic use of recursion: divide, conquer, and the call-tree cost.

title: Backtracking
summary: Build a solution incrementally and undo when a partial assignment cannot work.

title: Divide & Conquer
summary: Split, solve subproblems independently, combine. Recurrences describe the cost.

title: Greedy
summary: Commit to a locally optimal choice. Correct only when an exchange argument says so.

title: Dynamic Programming
summary: Optimal substructure plus overlapping subproblems: remember the answer instead of recomputing it.

title: Breadth-First Search
summary: Explore by distance from the source. Shortest paths in unweighted graphs.

title: Depth-First Search
summary: Explore a path to the end, then backtrack. Cycle detection, topology, components.

title: Topological Sort
summary: A linear order of a DAG so every edge goes forward. Build systems and course schedules.

title: Dijkstra's Algorithm
summary: Non-negative shortest paths via a greedy frontier and a priority queue.

title: Bellman-Ford
summary: Relax all edges |V|−1 times. Handles negative weights and reports negative cycles.

title: Floyd-Warshall
summary: All-pairs shortest paths by trying each vertex as an intermediate.

title: Kruskal's Algorithm
summary: MST by sorting edges and adding those that do not form a cycle (DSU).

title: Prim's Algorithm
summary: MST by growing a tree from a seed, always adding the cheapest leaving edge.

title: Bit Manipulation
summary: Using the binary representation: masks, shifts, and counting bits as constant-time tricks.

title: String Algorithms
summary: Matching, hashing, KMP, Z-function, and suffix structures for pattern search.

title: Randomized Algorithms
summary: Algorithms that flip coins: expected time, Monte Carlo vs Las Vegas, hashing.

title: Logic
summary: The rules of valid inference. Every spec, type system, and proof sits on it.

title: Propositional Logic
summary: Boolean variables and connectives. Truth tables, SAT, and circuit equivalence.

title: Predicate Logic
summary: Quantifiers over domains. This is the language of specifications and most proofs.

title: Sets
summary: Collections defined by membership. Union, intersection, power set, cardinality.

title: Relations
summary: Subsets of a product. Reflexive, symmetric, transitive — and the closures you take.

title: Functions
summary: Mappings from a domain to a codomain: injective, surjective, bijective, invertible.

title: Proofs
summary: Direct, contrapositive, contradiction, construction, and the habits that make arguments checkable.

title: Mathematical Induction
summary: Prove P(n0), assume P(k), prove P(k+1). Strong induction and structural induction included.

title: Combinatorics
summary: Counting: products, permutations, combinations, inclusion-exclusion, pigeonhole.

title: Probability
summary: Sample spaces, independence, expectation, and the inequalities used in algorithms.

title: Graph Theory
summary: The mathematics of graphs: connectivity, coloring, matching, planarity, cuts.

title: Trees (Math)
summary: Acyclic connected graphs. Spanning trees, rooted trees, and counting labeled trees.

title: Recurrence Relations
summary: Equations that define a sequence from earlier terms. Master theorem lives here.

title: Boolean Algebra
summary: Algebra of 0/1 with AND, OR, NOT. Normal forms, minimization, and hardware.

title: CPU
summary: The processor: fetch an instruction, decode it, execute it, repeat.

title: ALU
summary: The arithmetic-logic unit: adders, shifters, comparators, and flags.

title: Registers
summary: The fastest named storage in the CPU. Architectural vs microarchitectural.

title: Control Unit
summary: The logic that sequences fetch/decode/execute and drives datapath muxes.

title: Instruction Set Architecture
summary: The contract between software and hardware: opcodes, registers, addressing, memory model.

title: Machine Instructions
summary: The binary encoding of operations the CPU actually executes.

title: Assembly
summary: A human-readable form of machine code, with labels, directives, and addressing modes.

title: Memory Hierarchy
summary: Registers, caches, DRAM, disk — a pyramid that trades capacity for latency.

title: Cache
summary: Small fast memory that stores recently used blocks. Hits, misses, and associativity.

title: RAM
summary: Volatile main memory. DRAM cells, DIMMs, and why random access is not actually equal-cost.

title: ROM
summary: Read-mostly memory for firmware and bootstrap. Modern 'ROM' is often flash.

title: Storage
summary: Persistent devices: HDD, SSD, and the block interface the OS sees.

title: CPU Pipeline
summary: Overlapping fetch, decode, execute, memory, write-back so several instructions are in flight.

title: Branch Prediction
summary: Guessing the next PC so the pipeline does not stall on every if.

title: Multicore Processors
summary: Several cores on one die, sharing some caches and all of memory — and the problems that follow.

title: GPU
summary: A throughput processor: thousands of lanes, SIMT, and a memory system built for bandwidth.

title: SIMD
summary: One instruction, many data. Vector units, warps, and data-parallel loops.

title: DMA
summary: Devices that copy memory without occupying the CPU for every byte.

title: Interrupts (Hardware)
summary: An asynchronous signal that vectors the CPU into a handler, then returns.

title: Cache Coherence
summary: The protocol that keeps per-core caches from disagreeing about a line (MESI and friends).

title: NUMA
summary: Non-uniform memory access: local DRAM is faster than remote DRAM on another socket.

title: What is an OS?
summary: The program that multiplexes hardware and offers processes a usable machine.

title: Kernel
summary: The privileged core of the OS: syscalls, scheduling, virtual memory, drivers.

title: System Calls
summary: The trap into the kernel: the only legal way a user program asks for privileged work.

title: User Mode
summary: Unprivileged execution. Page faults and syscalls are how you leave it.

title: Kernel Mode
summary: Privileged execution: the CPU will honor instructions that touch control registers and I/O.

title: Processes
summary: An OS abstraction: address space, at least one thread, and a pile of kernel metadata.

title: Threads
summary: A schedulable execution context. Threads in one process share an address space.

title: Process States
summary: New, ready, running, waiting, terminated — and the events that move a process between them.

title: Context Switching
summary: Saving one thread's registers and loading another's so the CPU can change jobs.

title: CPU Scheduling
summary: The policy that picks the next ready thread. Fairness, latency, and throughput trade off.

title: FCFS
summary: First-come, first-served. Simple, convoy-prone, no preemption required.

title: SJF
summary: Shortest job first. Optimal average waiting time if you magically know run times.

title: Round Robin
summary: Time slices in a cycle. The quantum is the whole design.

title: Priority Scheduling
summary: Run the highest-priority ready thread. Starvation and aging come with it.

title: Synchronization
summary: Coordinating threads that share state so the result could have been sequential.

title: Race Conditions
summary: When the result depends on an unlucky interleaving of concurrent accesses.

title: Critical Sections
summary: Code that must run as if atomic with respect to other threads touching the same data.

title: Mutex
summary: Mutual exclusion: at most one holder. The lock you actually want most of the time.

title: Semaphore
summary: A counter with wait/signal. Mutexes are semaphores of 1; producer-consumer uses more.

title: Monitors
summary: A language-level construct: a mutex plus condition variables bundled with the data.

title: Deadlocks
summary: A cycle of waits. Coffman conditions, detection, and the ways out.

title: Deadlock Prevention
summary: Break a Coffman condition so a cycle cannot form: no hold-and-wait, preemption, ordering.

title: Deadlock Avoidance
summary: Admit a request only if the resulting state is safe. Banker's algorithm is the classic.

title: Banker's Algorithm
summary: Dijkstra's safety algorithm: pretend to allocate, see if a finish order exists.

title: Memory Management
summary: How the OS carves physical memory for processes: allocation, protection, sharing.

title: Paging
summary: Fixed-size pages and frames. The idea that makes virtual memory practical.

title: Segmentation
summary: Variable-sized logical regions (code, heap, stack) with base and limit.

title: Virtual Memory
summary: Each process sees its own address space, backed by RAM and disk as needed.

title: Page Tables
summary: The map from virtual page to frame (or disk). Multi-level to keep them sparse.

title: TLB
summary: A cache of page-table entries so every load does not walk the page table.

title: Page Replacement
summary: Which resident page to evict on a fault. The policy is the whole game.

title: LRU
summary: Replace the page unused for the longest time. Stack algorithms and clock approximations.

title: FIFO Replacement
summary: Evict the oldest page. Belady's anomaly is the interview sting.

title: Thrashing
summary: When the working set does not fit, the system spends its time paging, not computing.

title: File Systems
summary: The on-disk (and in-memory) structures that turn bytes into files, directories, and mounts.

title: Disk Scheduling
summary: FCFS, SSTF, SCAN — algorithms from the HDD era that still show up in interviews.

title: I/O
summary: How the kernel talks to devices: programmed I/O, interrupts, DMA, block vs character.

title: Interrupts (OS)
summary: The kernel's view: interrupt context, bottom halves, and why you cannot sleep in a handler.

title: Signals
summary: Software interrupts to a process: SIGINT, SIGCHLD, handlers, and async-signal-safety.

title: IPC
summary: Pipes, sockets, shared memory, message queues — how processes exchange data.

title: Linux Process Model
summary: Tasks, fork, clone, copy-on-write, namespaces, and cgroups as the real Unix.

title: What is Networking?
summary: Independent machines exchanging messages over a shared, unreliable medium.

title: LAN
summary: A local area network: one broadcast domain or a few, under one administration.

title: WAN
summary: A wide-area network spanning sites and usually several providers.

title: MAN
summary: A metropolitan network: a city-scale fabric, often provider-owned fiber.

title: PAN
summary: A personal area network: Bluetooth, USB, the devices around one person.

title: Network Topology
summary: Bus, star, ring, mesh, hybrid — how nodes are wired, logically and physically.

title: Client/Server
summary: A role split: clients initiate, servers wait and respond. Most of the internet.

title: Peer-to-Peer
summary: Nodes that are both client and server. BitTorrent, some overlay networks, some blockchains.

title: Network Devices
summary: The box-level view: hubs, switches, routers, firewalls, and where each sits in the stack.

title: Hub
summary: A physical-layer repeater: every bit out every port. Collision domain = the whole hub.

title: Switch
summary: A data-link device that forwards frames by MAC and splits collision domains.

title: Router
summary: A network-layer device that forwards packets between subnets using a routing table.

title: Bridge
summary: Connects two L2 segments and learns MACs. A switch is a multi-port bridge.

title: Gateway
summary: A node that translates between networks or protocols — often just 'the router'.

title: Repeater
summary: Amplifies or retimes a signal to extend a physical segment.

title: Modem
summary: Modulator-demodulator: analog carrier on, bits off, and the reverse.

title: Access Point
summary: A bridge between wireless stations and a wired LAN, with association and encryption.

title: Firewall
summary: A policy box: filter, NAT, or proxy traffic by rule. Host or network, stateful or not.

title: OSI Model
summary: Seven layers of function, from photons to application messages. The shared language of networking.

title: Layer 7 — Application
summary: The OSI layer where applications meet the network: HTTP, DNS, SMTP, and their data.

title: Layer 6 — Presentation
summary: Syntax and encryption: encoding, compression, TLS as it is often taught at this layer.

title: Layer 5 — Session
summary: Dialogs: setup, teardown, and checkpoints. Thin in TCP/IP, explicit in some RPC systems.

title: Layer 4 — Transport
summary: Process-to-process: ports, reliability, and congestion control. TCP and UDP live here.

title: Layer 3 — Network
summary: Host-to-host across hops: IP, routing, ICMP. Packets and logical addresses.

title: Layer 2 — Data Link
summary: Hop-to-hop frames: MAC addresses, Ethernet, switches, and error detection.

title: Layer 1 — Physical
summary: Bits on a medium: voltage, light, radio, connectors, and the limits of Shannon.

title: TCP/IP Model
summary: Four layers the internet actually runs: application, transport, internet, network access.

title: OSI vs TCP/IP
summary: A seven-layer teaching model versus a four-layer running model. Same ideas, different cuts.

title: Signals
summary: The physical representation of bits: analog vs digital, encoding, and noise.

title: Bandwidth
summary: How much spectrum or bit-rate a channel offers. Not the same thing as throughput.

title: Latency
summary: One-way or round-trip delay. Propagation, transmission, queueing, processing.

title: Transmission Media
summary: Copper, fiber, and wireless — each with a noise, cost, and distance story.

title: Fiber
summary: Light in glass. Huge bandwidth, long reach, immunity to electrical noise.

title: Copper
summary: Twisted pair and coax. Cheap, familiar, and still how most desks are wired.

title: Wireless
summary: Shared spectrum, fading, and a MAC that is nothing like a wire.

title: Modulation
summary: Imprinting bits on a carrier: AM, FM, PSK, QAM — the physical alphabet.

title: Frames
summary: The data-link PDU: header, payload, trailer. Ethernet's 14-byte header is the one you will draw.

title: MAC Addresses
summary: 48-bit link-layer identifiers. Unique-ish, local or universal, unicast or group.

title: Ethernet
summary: The LAN technology: CSMA/CD history, switching present, 802.3 framing.

title: Switching
summary: Learn MACs, flood unknowns, forward knowns, filter the rest. CAM tables and STP.

title: ARP
summary: Resolve IPv4 to MAC on a LAN. The cache, the timeout, and the spoof.

title: Error Detection
summary: Parity, checksums, CRC. Detecting corruption is cheaper than preventing it.

title: VLANs
summary: One physical switch, many broadcast domains. 802.1Q tags and trunk ports.

title: IP
summary: The internet's network protocol: best-effort datagrams and hierarchical addresses.

title: IPv4
summary: 32-bit addresses, dotted quad, fragmentation, and a header you should be able to sketch.

title: IPv6
summary: 128-bit addresses, no NAT-as-crutch, SLAAC, and a simpler header.

title: Subnetting
summary: Carving a prefix into smaller networks. Masks, hosts, and the all-zero/all-one rules.

title: CIDR
summary: Classless addressing: a prefix and a length. Aggregation is the point.

title: Routing
summary: Choosing a next hop. Tables, longest prefix match, and intra- vs inter-domain.

title: ICMP
summary: IP's control plane for errors and diagnostics. Ping and traceroute ride it.

title: NAT
summary: Rewriting addresses (and usually ports) so many hosts share a public IP.

title: Routing Protocols
summary: RIP, OSPF, BGP: how routers learn paths they did not configure by hand.

title: TCP
summary: Reliable, ordered, congestion-controlled byte streams between two ports.

title: UDP
summary: Datagrams with ports and a checksum. No connection, no retransmission, no congestion control.

title: Ports
summary: 16-bit transport addresses that multiplex a host. Well-known, registered, ephemeral.

title: TCP Handshake
summary: SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK. Sequence numbers exchanged so a connection can start.

title: TCP Teardown
summary: Four-way (or three-way with FIN-ACK) close, TIME-WAIT, and why half-open exists.

title: Flow Control
summary: Stopping a fast sender from drowning a slow receiver. TCP's window.

title: Congestion Control
summary: Protecting the network from collapse: slow start, AIMD, ECN, and BBR.

title: DNS
summary: The hierarchical lookup that turns names into records — usually addresses.

title: DHCP
summary: Automatic host configuration: address, mask, gateway, DNS, lease.

title: HTTP
summary: The application protocol of the web: methods, status codes, headers, and now HTTP/2 and /3.

title: HTTPS
summary: HTTP over TLS. Confidentiality, integrity, and (usually) server authentication.

title: FTP
summary: A historic file protocol with separate control and data channels. Prefer SFTP/HTTPS.

title: SMTP
summary: How mail moves between MTAs. Store-and-forward, MX records, and spam as an adversarial load.

title: SSH
summary: Authenticated, encrypted remote shells and tunnels. Keys, not passwords, if you can.

title: WebSockets
summary: A TCP-backed, full-duplex channel started with an HTTP upgrade.
